project_name: PortPulse — Container Congestion Predictor & Port Operations Optimiser
time_budget: flexible — good amount of time, not a fixed 24h sprint, but the prototype must stay simple, clean, and professional rather than over-scoped
mission: Build a working prototype that predicts port congestion before it happens, automatically reroutes vessels and reassigns berths/cranes to avoid it, and outputs a 72-hour operations plan a shift supervisor can actually act on. The demo must show a clear before/after: a congestion scenario forming, the system catching it early, and the measurable improvement (e.g. reduced average wait time) after optimization.

context_for_the_model.real_world_reference: 2021 LA/Long Beach port backlog: 100+ ships waiting offshore for weeks, $10B+ cost to global supply chains, caused by manual reactive spreadsheet-based berth/crane allocation and late-detected congestion.
context_for_the_model.core_insight: The failure mode being solved is REACTIVE detection (congestion spotted only after ships are already queuing). The product's entire value is in being PREDICTIVE and PRESCRIPTIVE, not just descriptive.

modules.name: data_simulation
modules.purpose: Generate a realistic synthetic dataset since no real dataset is provided.
requirements: Vessel schedule generator: arrival time (ETA), vessel size/class, cargo volume, priority level
Port capacity model: fixed number of berths (e.g. 8) with different size compatibility, fixed number of cranes (e.g. 20) with throughput rate per hour
Must be able to inject a deliberate congestion scenario (burst of arrivals, a berth going offline, a slow-unload vessel) so the demo has an obvious problem to solve
Output format: time-series data (CSV/JSON) covering a 72-hour rolling window

modules.name: congestion_prediction
modules.purpose: Predict which berths/time-windows will become bottlenecks before they occur.
requirements: Input: upcoming vessel arrivals + current berth/crane occupancy + historical throughput
Output: a congestion risk score per berth per time-slot over the next 72 hours

Approach: keep it simple and explainable — queue-length forecasting or regression is acceptable; do NOT over-invest in deep learning under a 24h budget. A model that visibly works beats a sophisticated one that doesn't run.
Must clearly flag WHEN a bottleneck will occur (not just that congestion exists)

modules.name: routing_and_optimization
modules.purpose: Given predicted bottlenecks, automatically resolve them.
requirements: Reroute vessels heading into a predicted bottleneck to an alternate available berth or delayed slot
Assign cranes to berths to minimize total vessel wait/turnaround time
Treat this as an assignment/scheduling optimization problem (greedy heuristic is acceptable fallback if a solver like OR-Tools CP-SAT is too time-costly to integrate)
Must produce a quantifiable improvement metric: average wait time before vs after optimization

modules.name: ops_plan_output
modules.purpose: Present the result as something a real shift supervisor could use.
requirements: 72-hour timeline view: which vessel is assigned to which berth/crane and when
Highlighted congestion-risk windows and what action was taken to avoid them
Summary metrics panel: vessels processed, average wait time, congestion incidents avoided
Must be visually clear in a live demo within 30-60 seconds of walkthrough

tech_stack.backend: Python (FastAPI or Flask) for simulation, prediction, and optimization logic
tech_stack.optimization: OR-Tools CP-SAT if time allows, otherwise a documented greedy/heuristic assignment algorithm
tech_stack.frontend: React/Next.js dashboard for the 72h ops plan and congestion visualization
tech_stack.dev_assistant: IBM Bob used throughout for scaffolding, boilerplate generation, and cross-module integration to maximize speed within the 24h window
tech_stack.data_storage: In-memory or flat-file (CSV/JSON) — no need for a persistent database given the time budget

in_scope: One coherent end-to-end pipeline: simulate -> predict -> optimize -> visualize
Synthetic but realistic data with an injectable congestion scenario
A simple, explainable, WORKING prediction approach
An optimizer that produces a measurable before/after improvement
A clean, demo-ready dashboard for the 72h plan
A 2-3 minute demo narrative built around the LA/Long Beach-style scenario
explicitly_out_of_scope: Real-time integration with actual port/AIS data feeds
User authentication, multi-tenant support, or production-grade infrastructure
Deep learning / large model training for prediction
Handling more than one port / multi-port network effects
Anything not directly demoable within 2-3 minutes

success_criteria_for_judging: Does the system clearly PREDICT congestion before it happens (not just report current state)?
Does the optimization step produce a visible, quantified improvement (e.g. wait time reduced X%)?
Is the 72h ops plan output something a real port operator would find usable and understandable in seconds?
Does the demo tell a clear story: problem (LA/Long Beach-style backlog) -> prediction -> automated fix -> measurable result?
Is the prototype actually running live, not just slides/mockups?

risk_mitigation.if_running_low_on_time: Cut model sophistication before cutting the end-to-end pipeline. A simple rule-based predictor with a working optimizer and a clean dashboard beats a fancy ML model with no visible output.
risk_mitigation.fallback_optimizer: If OR-Tools integration proves too time-costly, use a greedy nearest-available-berth heuristic and clearly document it as a v1 approach with CP-SAT noted as the next step.
risk_mitigation.demo_safety_net: Pre-generate and cache at least one known-good congestion scenario + result set in case live computation is slow or flaky during the actual demo.

folder_structure..github/workflows/: optional CI (lint + basic test run on PR) — skip if it eats setup time
folder_structure.data/raw/: generated synthetic vessel/port data (gitignore if large)
folder_structure.data/schema.md: field definitions for vessels, berths, cranes
folder_structure.demo/scenario_congested.json: pre-baked known-good congestion scenario — the fallback if live compute is slow during judging
folder_structure.demo/demo_script.md: timed walkthrough script for the live demo
folder_structure.demo/screen_recording.mp4: backup recording in case the live demo fails
folder_structure.docs/decisions.md: running log of tradeoff calls and why (e.g. greedy heuristic over CP-SAT because X)
folder_structure.docs/assumptions.md: explicit note that data is synthetic + documented scope cuts, for judges' follow-up questions
folder_structure.presentation/README.md: keep — notes tying slides to repo
folder_structure.presentation/slides.pdf: exported pitch deck, not just a live Google Slides link
folder_structure.src/simulation/: synthetic data generator — owned by Person A
folder_structure.src/prediction/: congestion prediction module — owned by Person A
folder_structure.src/optimization/: routing + berth/crane assignment — owned by Person B
folder_structure.src/api/: backend wiring modules together — owned by Person D
folder_structure.src/dashboard/: frontend 72h ops plan visualization — owned by Person C
folder_structure.src/shared/: single source of truth for types/schemas (e.g. Vessel, Berth, Crane) used by every module — never redefine these per-module
folder_structure.tests/: focused unit tests for prediction and optimization logic (3-4 tests is enough to signal real engineering process)
folder_structure..env.example: config template — never commit real secrets
folder_structure.README.md: single source of truth for how to run the project — update immediately whenever setup steps change
folder_structure.submission.yaml: keep — verify its schema matches the hackathon's actual submission requirements before final submit

file_ownership_rules: One folder, one owner: Person A owns src/simulation + src/prediction, Person B owns src/optimization, Person C owns src/dashboard, Person D owns src/api and cross-module integration
src/shared/ is the only place shared types/schemas are defined — redefining a type in two modules is the top source of integration bugs under time pressure
Cross-module changes go through a quick PR/review, not a direct push into someone else's folder
commit_and_docs_discipline: Commit small and often (e.g. 'feat(prediction): add queue-length scorer') rather than one giant end-of-day commit, so a single broken piece can be rolled back without losing everything
Add a line to docs/decisions.md at the moment a tradeoff is made, not retroactively — takes 30 seconds and prevents scrambling before the pitch
Update README.md the moment setup/run steps change so anyone can clone and run in under 5 minutes
pre_submission_checklist: Run demo/demo_script.md end-to-end at least twice
Confirm demo/scenario_congested.json and the backup screen recording both still work
Clean out any unfinished/speculative files from src/ and demo/ — a smaller working repo beats a larger messy one
Verify submission.yaml matches the organizer's actual required schema

team_roles.person_d: Backend integration, IBM Bob-assisted scaffolding across modules, demo narrative and pitch prep

deliverables: Working end-to-end prototype (runnable, not just slides)
3-5 slide pitch deck: problem -> solution -> demo -> impact/metrics
Live 2-3 minute demo script rehearsed by at least one team member
One-paragraph README explaining assumptions (synthetic data, scope cuts) for judges who ask follow-up questions
